name: Temple Crag and Mount Gayley
region: Sierra Nevada, Palisades (South Fork Big Pine Creek)

legs.route: Contact Crack (5.2) from Contact Pass, or the southeast face chute to the summit ridge; Moon Goddess Arete is the long roped alternative
Ridge from Glacier Notch, class 3 on solid blocks just right of the crest
legs.connect: Drop back toward the South Fork drainage, then climb the big gully beside the north faces to the glacier and Glacier Notch; usually a separate day or a long afternoon push.

duration: 2-3 days from the South Fork trailhead
how: Both summits sit above the same drainage, so parties base in the South Fork valley and climb them on successive days, or tag Gayley the same afternoon if energy allows. Temple Crag is the more technical outing: a short fifth-class crack or a second-class face with an exposed notch near the top, versus a multi-pitch arete. Gayley is a class 3 ridge scramble from the notch above the glacier, with only a snowfield or an easy bergschrund crossing on the way.
descent: Return from Temple Crag the way you came up, through the pass and lake basins. From Gayley, descend the glacier gully toward the lakes, which is much quicker than the long meadow route.
logistics: Trailhead is the South Fork of Big Pine Creek; an overnight permit and bear canister are needed. Camp near the upper lakes below the face. Summer to early fall; the glacier gully may hold hard snow early.
notes: Three independent trips. Only one climber in the 2005 report added Gayley the same day as Temple Crag; the 1996 report does not say whether the two were same-day. Gayley route (class 3 ridge from Glacier Notch) is from the 1996 and 2005 reports.

name: Mount Kaweah, Black Kaweah and Red Kaweah
region: Sierra Nevada, Kaweah Peaks (Sequoia National Park, Big Arroyo)

legs.route: Class 2 talus and sand from the valley side
Southwest face: ramp and chute system, class 3 with a short steeper wall
legs.connect: Return to the high camp above the valley, then climb the next morning up the chutes below the peak.

legs.route: Main chute then left branch, class 2 with a few low class 3 moves, finishing up the north ridge
legs.connect: Another morning from the same high camp via the chutes beside Black Kaweah.

how: Parties cross the Great Western Divide from Mineral King, drop to the broad valley at its base, and set a high camp on the slopes beneath the three peaks. Each summit is then a separate day trip from that camp, with the class 2 hike up Mount Kaweah the easiest. Black is the hardest of the trio, with a steep chute and a short fifth-class section on some lines; Red is mostly boulder climbing.
descent: Each peak is descended by its own approach to camp. The exit retraces the two passes back to the trailhead; no new technical ground is added.
logistics: Trailhead is Mineral King; an overnight permit is needed, with bear storage. Typical camps are a lake basin the first night and an exposed camp near 11,500 ft above the valley. Summer to early fall.
notes: The second source is a guided ridge traverse that starts from the same valley base camp and ends on Mount Kaweah; it confirms the three peaks as one outing and the class 2 Kaweah finish, not the separate day-trip format. Black Kaweah: one report says class 3 with a short 5th-class wall, the traverse report says 4th to low 5th.

name: Mount Hoffmann and Tuolumne Peak

legs.route: South slope from May Lake (class 2), or the east side with class 3 steps
Southeast slopes, class 2 (a short class 3 south face is the alternative)
legs.connect: Cross the summit plateau and follow the northeast ridge down, class 3-4 blocky scrambling with a chimney and a knife edge, then easier talus to Tuolumne Peak. Other parties go the opposite way along the ridge over lower bumps.

how: Both peaks rise above May Lake and are tied by one ridge, so climbers go up one and along to the other in a loop. The direct ridge between them is harder than either summit alone; a gentler option is the broad ridge crest with a lower west-side bypass of the knife edge. Taking Hoffmann by its trail and Tuolumne by its easy slopes keeps the day mostly class 2.
descent: Walk down Tuolumne's southeast slopes to rejoin the trail past the High Sierra camp, or finish by descending Hoffmann's trail. Either way you end at the May Lake parking lot.
logistics: Start and end at the May Lake trailhead off Tioga Road; no overnight needed. Mosquitoes in midsummer and snow on the trail in early season.
notes: The two reports run opposite directions and describe different connections (northeast ridge class 3-4 vs ridge crest with a class 2 bypass). The higher class is stated in the text.

name: Mount Stanford to Mount Morgan (north) traverse

legs.route: East slope from the Hilton Creek lake basin, class 2 with easy class 3 near the top
Ridge over several high points, then the talus fan to the north summit
legs.connect: Follow the roughly one-mile ridge southward, staying on the crest over snow, drop to the broad saddle and climb the rocky slope to the north summit.

how: From the Hilton Lakes trail, leave the lake basin for Stanford's east slope, then follow the crest to Morgan. The ridge is rated class 3, though some parties find it easier with a little exposure and one possible class 3 move. Morgan has two high points; the north one is higher. It makes a loop that needs no car shuttle.
descent: Go down the sandy southeast slope or a gully just south of the top, glissading snow if present, then through aspens above the lake and back to the trail. Cliff bands lie above the lake, so pick the line carefully.
logistics: Hilton Lakes trailhead across from Rock Creek Lake; one party camped about 4 miles in near 10,300 ft, another did it as a long day. An overnight permit applies if camping; late spring snow or fall are common windows.
notes: Both reports rate the ridge class 3. Day length differs with camp choice.
